\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:hardytailaggregationsharp}]
Proposition~\ref{prop:hardytailaggregation} gives the upper bound.
For the reverse bound, fix a finite family
$v^{(j)}\in[0,\infty)^n$ with $c:=\sum_{j=1}^mv^{(j)}\le a$
and $0<\varepsilon<1$. Set
\[
 \forall j\in[m]:\qquad s_j:=p\varepsilon^{j-1},\qquad s_{m+1}:=0.
\]
Let $U$ be uniform on $(0,1)$ and, for $0<u<1$, define
\[
 q_i^\varepsilon(u):=
 a_i-c_i+\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{p\,v_i^{(j)}}{s_j}\mathbf1_{(0,s_j)}(u),
 \qquad X_i^\varepsilon:=q_i^\varepsilon(U).
\]
These variables are nonnegative, finite-valued, and comonotone.
Their quantile operators $\TT[X_i^\varepsilon]$ are the maximal
completions of the decreasing step profiles $q_i^\varepsilon$ on $(0,1)$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:hardy} and scalar integration give
\[
 \mathcal H(\TT[X_i^\varepsilon])(p)
 =\frac1p\int_0^p\TT[X_i^\varepsilon](u)\,du
 =a_i-c_i+\sum_{j=1}^mv_i^{(j)}=a_i.
\]
Write $q^\varepsilon=(q_1^\varepsilon,\ldots,q_n^\varepsilon)$.
On $(s_{j+1},s_j)$ one has
$q^\varepsilon(u)\ge p\,v^{(j)}/s_j$.
The completed quantile representation for comonotone variables,
monotonicity, and homogeneity therefore give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal H\left(

If $h$ is maximal, Minty's theorem gives $\ran(h+\id)=\R$, and
$\ran(h+\id)\subseteq\dom h+\ran h$
proves \eqref{eq:domainrange}.
Conversely, suppose that $\ran(h+\id)$ is an interval and $\dom h+\ran h=\R$.
For $t=x+v\in\dom h+\ran h$, choose $u\in h(x)$ and $y\in h^{-1}(v)$.
If $x<y$, monotonicity gives $u\le v$, hence $x+u\le x+v\le y+v$;
if $x>y$, it gives $u\ge v$, hence $y+v\le x+v\le x+u$;
and if $x=y$, then $t=y+v$ is itself one of the bounding values.
Thus
\[
 \min\{x+u,y+v\}\le t=x+v\le\max\{x+u,y+v\}.
\]
Both bounding values belong to $\ran(h+\id)$, so $t\in\ran(h+\id)$.
Hence $\ran(h+\id)=\dom h+\ran h=\R$,
and Minty's theorem proves maximality.
Applying this characterization to $-h$ gives the nonincreasing case.

\begin{proposition}[Composition]\label{prop:composition}
Let $f,g$ be maximal with orientations $\sigma,\tau\in\{1,-1\}$, where $1$ denotes nondecreasing, and suppose $g\circ f\ne\varnothing$. The composite is monotone with the expected orientation $\varepsilon=\sigma\tau$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rectangle}
 \forall z\in\R:\qquad
 f^{-1}(z)\text{ or }g(z)\text{ has at most one element}.
\end{equation}
Under this condition,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compositionmax}
 g\circ f\text{ is maximal in orientation }\varepsilon
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \dom f+\varepsilon\ran g=\R.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Distinct intermediate values order the endpoints of the composite in orientation $\sigma\tau$. Equal intermediate values cause no obstruction precisely when \eqref{eq:rectangle} holds: otherwise $f^{-1}(z)\times g(z)$ contains a nondegenerate rectangle, which is not monotone in either orientation. Reindexing the intermediate variable gives
\[
 \ran\bigl(\id+\varepsilon(g\circ f)\bigr)
 =\ran(f^{-1}+\varepsilon g)
 =\dom f+\varepsilon\ran g.
\]
The two summands have orientation $\sigma$ and nonempty common domain. Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:sums} and Minty's criterion.
\end{proof}
For example, take $f(0)=(-\infty,0]$; for $x>0$, set $f(x)=\{0\}$, and for $x<0$, set $f(x)=\varnothing$. Then $f\in\Mu$ but, for every $x\geq0$, $(f\circ f)(x)=(-\infty,0]$, so the composite is not monotone. The qualification in \eqref{eq:rectangle} cannot be suppressed.

statement_tex:
To study nonnegative products, we first record a consequence of the composition criterion.
For a nonnegative operator $k$, write
\[
 (\log k)(x)=\{\log u:u\in k(x),\ u>0\}.
\]
\begin{lemma}[Maximality under logarithms]\label{lem:logmaximal}
Let $f:\R\rightrightarrows\R$ be maximally monotone in either orientation.
If $\ran f\subset[0,\infty)$ and there exists $c>0$ with $c\in\ran f$,
then $\log f$ is maximally monotone with the same orientation.
\end{lemma}
If $\ran f=\{0\}$, then $\gra(\log f)=\varnothing$, so $\log f$ is not maximal.
\begin{proof}
The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\R$ is a single-valued maximal
nondecreasing operator. The positive-range hypothesis makes
$\log\circ f$ nonempty. The rectangle condition in
Proposition~\ref{prop:composition} is automatic, and
$\dom f+\sigma\ran(\log)=\R$, where $\sigma$ is the
orientation of $f$. That proposition proves maximality.
\end{proof}

statement_tex:
\begin{proposition}[Lower bound for the moment scale]
\label{prop:local-moment-sharpness}
Let $q_\Delta,q_1,\ldots,q_n$ satisfy the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{the:concentration_bounded_variations}.
There exist a metric space $E$, an $E$-valued random vector $Z$,
measurable controls $\Lambda_i$, and a scalar map $\Phi:E\to\R$
satisfying \eqref{eq:local-modulus} and \eqref{eq:local-input}
with these profiles, such that for every $r>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-moment-lower}
 \bigl\|\Phi(Z)-\Phi(Z')\bigr\|_{L^r}
 \geq2^{-1/r}
       \left\|q_\Delta\prod_iq_i\right\|_{L^r(I)}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
The coefficient $2^{-1/r}$ in this universal lower guarantee is
optimal for $r\geq1$. Indeed, take
$q_\Delta=q_1=\cdots=q_n=1$ on $I$ and consider any admissible
scalar map $\Phi$. On the common full-measure set
$A=\bigcap_i\{\Lambda_i\leq1\}$, the modulus
\eqref{eq:local-modulus} makes $\Phi$ $1$-Lipschitz.
A McShane extension from $A$ to $E$, followed by
\eqref{eq:local-input}, gives $|V-V'|\leq1$ almost surely for
$V=\Phi(Z)$. Independence then forces the essential range of $V$
to have diameter at most $1$. After translation, $V\in[0,1]$
almost surely, and its distribution function $F_V$ satisfies
\[
 \forall r\geq1:\qquad
 \E\left[|V-V'|^r\right]\leq\E\left[|V-V'|\right]
 =2\int_0^1F_V(t)(1-F_V(t))\,dt\leq\frac12.
\]
The equiprobable Bernoulli law on $\{0,1\}$, realized by the
construction in Section~\ref{app:local-moment} for these constant
profiles, attains $1/2$.
Thus no larger coefficient can hold in the universal lower guarantee.

statement_tex:
Our second application uses geometric Hardy averaging to control
nonlinear observations with random Lipschitz bounds. For a positive
nonincreasing operator $f$ on $(0,1)$ with integrable logarithm, define
\[
 \mathcal G(f)(p)
 =\exp\bigl(\mathcal H(\log\circ f)(p)\bigr)
 =\exp\left(\frac1p\int_0^p\log f(s)\,ds\right).
\]
This is the geometric mean operator in the classical P\'olya--Knopp
inequality \cite{HardyLittlewoodPolya1952,Luor2008GeometricMean};
Definition~\ref{def:geometrichardytransform} also treats zeros and
values at domain endpoints. Let $Z$ take values in a metric space $(E,d_E)$,
and let $Z'$ be an independent copy. Let $\TT_\Delta$ be a maximally
nonincreasing operator with domain interior $(0,1)$ and nonnegative
values there, such that
\[
 \forall f:E\to\R\text{ $1$-Lipschitz}:\qquad
 \TT[|f(Z)-f(Z')|]\leq\TT_\Delta.
\]
Such uniform control of Lipschitz observables is a standard conclusion
of concentration of measure theory. For example, if
$Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)$ in Euclidean space, Gaussian concentration
\cite[Proposition~5.34]{Vershynin2012Introduction} allows the choice
\[
 \forall u\in(0,1):\qquad \TT_\Delta(u)=2\sqrt{\log(2/u)},
\]
with maximal decreasing completion at the endpoints.\footnote{For this
choice, the quantile comparison is equivalent to requiring, for every
$t\geq0$ and every real $1$-Lipschitz function $f$,
$\PP(|f(Z)-f(Z')|\geq t)\leq2\exp(-t^2/4)$. The exponent follows by applying
Gaussian concentration to $(z,z')\mapsto f(z)-f(z')$, which has mean
zero and Lipschitz constant $\sqrt{2}$.}

statement_tex:
The following bounds are further consequences of these universal properties.
\begin{proposition}[Order bounds for extrema]\label{prop:extremaoperations}
Let $A$ be nonempty and $(f_a)_{a\in A}\in\Mu^A$.
Let $\Phi$ assign to each $f\in\Mu$ a set-valued operator $\Phi(f):\R\rightrightarrows\R$.
Assume that:
\[
 \forall f,g\in\Mu\text{ such that }\Phi(f),\Phi(g)\in\Mu,\qquad
 f\leq g\ \Longrightarrow\ \Phi(f)\leq\Phi(g).
\]
Whenever the displayed operators and extrema belong to $\Mu$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:extremaineq}
 \Phi(\inf_a f_a)\leq\inf_a\Phi(f_a),\qquad
 \sup_a\Phi(f_a)\leq\Phi(\sup_a f_a).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
The same conclusions hold with $\Mu$ replaced by $\Md$.
The bounds also hold when $\Phi$ sends one orientation class to the other and preserves the pointwise resolvent order, with extrema taken in the corresponding classes.
For example, $\Phi(f)=f\circ(-\id)$ sends $\Mu$ to $\Md$ and preserves the order and both extrema.
If instead $\Phi$ reverses the pointwise resolvent order, meaning that, whenever the images belong to the target class, $f\leq g$ implies $\Phi(f)\geq\Phi(g)$, the bounds become
\[
 \sup_a\Phi(f_a)\leq\Phi(\inf_a f_a),\qquad
 \Phi(\sup_a f_a)\leq\inf_a\Phi(f_a).
\]
Examples are inversion on $\Mu$, left composition by a decreasing operator whenever the composites are maximal, and $\Phi(f)=-f$.
Inversion on $\Md$ preserves the pointwise resolvent order, as stated in~\eqref{eq:inverseorder}.
\begin{proof}
The inequalities follow from the universal properties of infimum and supremum~\eqref{eq:universal_property_sup} and the assumed preservation or reversal of the pointwise resolvent order.
\end{proof}

title: One-sided derivatives of the expected-shortfall objective
notes: An arbitrary original probability space, measurable integrable real X, every positive p (hence 0<p<1) and every real threshold a. Neither an atomless law nor differentiability of the pointwise positive part at an atom is assumed. The finite real objective is convex. Its actual HasDerivWithinAt derivatives on Iio a and Ioi a are respectively 1-P(X>=a)/p and 1-P(X>a)/p. Thus the left derivative retains the atom at a and the right derivative excludes it. All expectations are on the original space. The positive-part difference quotient is bounded in absolute value by one for every threshold pair. Pointwise right/left limits are the strict/weak tail indicators, including the equality case X=a. Filter dominated convergence transfers these limits to expectations. Integrability discharges subtraction and normalization identities, and the pinned slope/derivative equivalence proves the actual one-sided derivatives. A direct integral convexity proof establishes the finite convex objective without assuming the desired subdifferential. Author correspondence review recorded on 2026-11-09.

statement_tex:
\begin{proof}
Fix $0<p<1$. The finite convex objective
$\Phi_p(a):=a+p^{-1}\E\left[(X-a)_+\right]$ has one-sided derivatives
\[
 \Phi'_{p,-}(a)=1-p^{-1}\PP(X\ge a),\qquad
 \Phi'_{p,+}(a)=1-p^{-1}\PP(X>a).
\]
Here $\partial\Phi_p$ denotes the ordinary convex subdifferential,
whose interval endpoints are the left and right derivatives:
\[
 \partial\Phi_p(a)
 =[\Phi'_{p,-}(a),\Phi'_{p,+}(a)]
 =1-p^{-1}\SSS[X](a).
\]
Thus
\[
 0\in\partial\Phi_p(a)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\in\SSS[X](a)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\in\TT[X](p).
\]
Since $\TT[X](p)$ is nonempty, $\Phi_p$ attains its minimum exactly
on this set, including when the minimizer is nonunique.

title: The hypersimplex is the convex hull of fixed-cardinality zero-one vectors
notes: For every natural n,k, the slice [0,1]^n with coordinate sum k has exactly the binary points of that sum as its extreme points, equals their convex hull, and admits an explicit finite convex decomposition with nonnegative weights summing to one. The integer sum excludes a single fractional coordinate; two fractional coordinates admit opposite perturbations. The pinned compact-convex theorem and finiteness of binary vertices give the actual convex hull, not merely its closure. The full median-transform assembly is now supplied separately by MedianTransform. Author correspondence review recorded on 2026-11-09.

statement_tex:
If $t=0$, the reverse inequality follows from $M^\sharp(a)\geq0$.
Suppose henceforth that $t>0$ and set
\[
 b_i:=\min(a_i,t).
\]
Then
\[
 \frac bt
 \in
 \left\{
 x\in[0,1]^n:
 \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=r+1
 \right\}.
\]
A point with two coordinates strictly between $0$ and $1$ admits
opposite small perturbations of those coordinates that preserve the sum,
so it is not an extreme point. The integer sum excludes exactly one
fractional coordinate. Conversely, the $0$--$1$ vectors in this polytope
are vertices of the cube and remain extreme points. Thus its extreme
points are precisely $\mathbbm{1}_I$ with $|I|=r+1$. Hence
\[
 b
 =
 \sum_jw_j\mathbbm{1}_{I_j},
 \qquad
 w_j\ge0,
 \qquad
 |I_j|=r+1,
 \qquad
 \sum_jw_j=t.
\]
Since $b\le a$, this family is admissible in
\eqref{eq:superadditivetransform}. Each vector $w_j\mathbbm{1}_{I_j}$ has
median $w_j$, so
\[
 M^\sharp(a)
 \ge
 \sum_jM(w_j\mathbbm{1}_{I_j})
 =
 \sum_jw_j
 =
 t.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:mediantransform}.
\end{proof}
